title: Twenty-Five Years After 9/11, U.S. Begins Rolling Back Travel Restrictions
excerpt: From the end of the shoes-off rule to water bottles for PreCheck members and gate access at 13 airports, a quarter century after the attacks the U.S. is easing the checkpoint rituals that defined a generation of travel.
body:
• A quarter century after the September 11, 2001 attacks, the U.S. has begun easing some of the airport security rules that reshaped air travel — from the shoes-off requirement, lifted in 2025, to gate access for non-ticketed visitors.
  • The TSA is reportedly considering letting some PreCheck members carry full water bottles through checkpoints at airports equipped with new CT scanners, though the 3-1-1 liquids rule remains in force nationwide.
  • A new "Gateside" program now allows non-passengers to go through security to departure gates at 13 U.S. airports, reviving a pre-9/11 ritual of tearful farewells and welcomes.
  • The changes coincide with the 25th anniversary of 9/11, observed on September 11 — and arrive just as the busy holiday travel season approaches.

A Quarter Century of Checkpoint Rituals

For almost 25 years, the American airport experience has followed a script written in the aftermath of September 11, 2001: shoes off, liquids in a quart-sized bag, and no family members beyond the security line. Now, as the country marks the 25th anniversary of the attacks, that script is being quietly rewritten. The U.S. government has started rolling back several of the most familiar post-9/11 travel restrictions, driven less by a change in threat assessment than by new screening technology that makes some of the old rituals unnecessary.

CNBC reported the shift on September 11, framing it as one of the anniversary's most tangible legacies: measures that defined a generation of travel are being eased one by one, from what passengers wear at checkpoints to what they can carry through them — and who is allowed to walk them to the gate.

Shoes Stay On, Water Bottles May Follow

The most visible change came last year, when the Department of Homeland Security ended the requirement that travellers remove their shoes at security checkpoints. The rule dated to 2006 — imposed after intelligence pointed to a continuing threat from the December 2001 attempt by Richard Reid, the so-called shoe bomber, to ignite explosives hidden in his footwear on a Paris-to-Miami flight.

Liquids could be next, at least for some travellers. ABC News and CBS News have reported that the TSA is considering allowing some PreCheck members to take full water bottles through security at selected airports equipped with newer computed tomography (CT) scanners capable of detecting liquid contents. ABC cited the TSA administrator; CBS cited senior administration officials, who said the change could arrive at a select number of airports in the coming months.

Officials are stressing limits, not a revolution. Former TSA head John Pistole told The New York Times the change is not expected to take effect until after the holiday travel season, and that it is unclear which airports would participate first. The 3-1-1 rule — containers of 3.4 ounces or less inside a single quart-sized bag — remains the law of the checkpoint everywhere for now. That rule, in force since August 2006, was itself a response to a foiled British plot to detonate liquid explosives on transatlantic flights; the TSA initially banned all liquids before settling on the 3-1-1 compromise.

"TSA will continue to explore opportunities to enhance security and improve the traveling experience for the public. As technology evolves, TSA's multi-layered security protocols will evolve, including benefits for our most trusted travelers."

— TSA, in a statement to the press

Back to the Gate

The most emotionally resonant change may be the least technological. Before 9/11, family members and friends without boarding passes could walk travellers to the gate — the cinematic farewell and the arrival-gate welcome were ordinary parts of American life. The attacks ended that overnight.

Now, the "Gateside by TSA PreCheck" program, which debuted across 13 U.S. airports last week, is bringing a version of it back: vetted non-passengers can pass through security to meet arriving travellers or see off departing ones at the gate. It is a small program with outsized symbolism — a quarter century later, the airport is becoming a public space again.

How We Got Here

The post-9/11 security apparatus was built in layers, each responding to a specific attempted attack. The TSA itself began screening passengers at Baltimore/Washington International Airport in April 2002. Full-body scanners — officially advanced imaging technology — were deployed from early 2010 after a passenger tried to detonate an explosive device hidden in his underwear on an Amsterdam-to-Detroit flight in December 2009. PreCheck, the trusted-traveller program now central to the rollbacks, launched in 2011. Today the agency screens roughly 2.5 million passengers a day at more than 430 airports.

What It Means for Diaspora Travellers

For the Indian diaspora — among the most frequent long-haul flyers in the United States — the changes land at a practical moment. Diwali travel season is weeks away, and anyone who has watched an elderly parent struggle with shoes, belts and a quart bag of toiletries at 5 a.m. will recognise the shoe-rule rollback as a genuine quality-of-life improvement. The water-bottle exception, if it materialises, matters most for families travelling with children. And for immigrants whose goodbyes have, for 25 years, ended at the security line, the return of gateside farewells is more than a procedural tweak — it is the recovery of a ritual.

What's Next

Watch the pilot airports: the water-bottle exception will stand or fall on whether CT scanners prove reliable at distinguishing water from other liquids at scale. The TSA has acknowledged it does not yet have enough suitable equipment — or funding — for a nationwide rollout. Any formal policy change will be announced through official channels, the agency says, and travellers should not assume the old rules are gone until it says so. The direction, though, is unmistakable: the checkpoint of 2026 is starting to look less like the checkpoint of 2002.
